deck: Lock & Lock — Security Detection & Response and Automated Financial Ops

slides.notes: Hello, I'm Junhan Shin, team lead of TEAM 1, Lock & Lock. We built “LockBank,” a system that detects and responds to security events for a financial service and automates operations end to end. I'll begin the presentation now.
The presentation will proceed in the following order: project overview, process and methodology, system architecture, actual results and demo, troubleshooting/debugging, and finally self-assessment.
First, the project overview.

Our topic was about detecting and responding to security events for a financial service and automating operations.
We aimed to proactively defend against the 3 core incidents with the greatest impact in a security breach: abnormal logins, API flooding, and container failures.
In particular, we built and validated infrastructure with self-healing capability for a financial domain that demands strict availability.
Our goal was to build a security-friendly infrastructure that addresses the 3 core incidents with the greatest impact among the various security incidents that commonly occur.
We also aimed to build an automated system with built-in self-healing capability to improve operational efficiency around security events.

Our planning intent rests on three pillars: building a security-first financial environment, detecting and alerting on threats or failures in real time, and creating high-availability infrastructure based on self-healing.
Security, Monitoring, and Self-Healing are the three core pillars.
Design an AWS financial infrastructure (VPC, private subnets) that minimizes external exposure, and linked static/dynamic security verification (Bandit, Trivy, OWASP ZAP) at the CI/CD stage with Blue-Green deployment to block vulnerabilities from ever reaching production.
Block and throttle critical financial security events such as abnormal logins and API traffic floods in real time via fail2ban and Nginx rate limiting, and immediately alert administrators through Alertmanager the moment anomalies occur.
Unify infrastructure and app metrics (Prometheus, CloudWatch) when a container or app failure occurs into a single view (Grafana) while the Recovery Controller auto-recovers within 5 minutes (RTO/RPO of 5 minutes) to minimize service downtime.

Our tech stack is centered on IaC, organized into development/collaboration, infrastructure/containers, monitoring/alerting, and automation.
Core tools included Terraform, Docker, Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Telegram, and the security scanner ZAP.
• Development & Collaboration: VS Code, GitHub, Google Drive, Notion
• Infrastructure & Containers: Terraform, Ansible, Docker CLI
• Monitoring & Alerting: Prometheus, Grafana, Telegram Bot
• Automation: GitHub Actions
Next is team structure and roles.

We split our team’s responsibilities into 5 parts, named A through E.
Track A owned the full Terraform-based AWS infrastructure and IaC; B covered the app and DB; C covered CI/CD; D covered monitoring and recovery; and E covered the security scenario.
A key feature was designing clear interfaces so each track's deliverables connected cleanly to the others.
Let me walk through our process and methodology.

We ran a 4-week schedule.
Week 1: topic selection and architecture design. Week 2: infrastructure build and app/DB implementation. Week 3: monitoring and security scenario implementation. Week 4: final review, demo flow testing, demo recording, and presentation preparation.

We ran Git collaboration in 3 stages. First, a **3-tier branch model (Feature → Dev → Main)** with role-based prefixes prevented conflicts. Second, we blocked direct pushes and required a rule where merging only happens after at least 1 approval and all review comments are resolved.
A key differentiator was automating first-pass code review with the Gemini Review Bot.

Per-track working branches (feature/<track>-<topic>): Prefixes for a(infrastructure), b(app), c(CI), d(monitoring), and e(security) clearly marked each role area to prevent collaboration conflicts

We followed a PR-based iterative development process from issue to deployment.
After defining a feature, we created a feature branch, followed commit conventions, and on opening a PR, went through **automated CI checks (build/security scan)** and Gemini review before integrating into dev, verifying E2E, and merging to main.
Now, the system architecture.

This is the overall architecture from the design phase. It's a hybrid structure linking AWS in the cloud with on-premises infrastructure, flowing as a single path from user requests through monitoring, security, and recovery.
We maximized security by isolating the Public zone connected to the outside internet (Route 53, ALB, Bastion, NAT) from the Private zone (App, DB).
Through a multi-AZ design (AZ-a, AZ-c) and Auto Scaling Group (ASG), we built high-availability infrastructure that guarantees financial service continuity even during server outages or traffic surges.
For data safety, we adopted a Main DB (EC2) and Replica structure.

From the user's perspective, requests pass through the ALB to app instances in the Auto Scaling group, with Nginx in front acting as the single entry point and first line of defense.
Client → Route 53 → IGW → ALB → Private Subnet (App server)
Users have no way of knowing the real IP of internal servers because they can only enter securely through Route 53 and the ALB.
All user traffic is encrypted over HTTPS (port 443) via ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) integration.

Administrator's perspective
Administrators bypass the public internet entirely and access internal infrastructure only through a Tailscale tunnel.
When a failure or threshold breach occurs, CloudWatch triggers an ASG scale-out to self-heal by expanding server capacity, sends alerts via the on-prem Grafana dashboard and Telegram notifications, and administrators can control the situation in real time.
For stability, internal data is automatically backed up to S3, AWS's durable storage, via periodic pg_dump.

In the case of when Blue-Green zero-downtime deployment is implemented (future work).
The goal is for the CI/CD workflow (runner) to pre-deploy new-version code to the Green environment, then switch routing to serve traffic without downtime. If a bug is found, it would immediately revert the load balancer back to Blue, which enables a fully automated zero-downtime rollback.
We designed the structure for Blue-Green zero-downtime deployment, but we separated it out as future work since it still needs stabilization testing. We'll cover this in more detail in the demo section later.

This is the container diagram. It shows how the app, DB, monitoring, and security containers are designed.
At the container level, the app, DB, monitoring, and security components each run as independent containers, connected over the Tailscale network.

The defining feature of our infrastructure is the hybrid setup.
We connected the on-prem Rocky8 server with the AWS cloud via Tailscale, so they operate as though they are on the same network.
The Replica DB and monitoring live on-prem while core services live in the cloud.
A hybrid setup connecting on-premises and AWS directly via Tailscale:
On-premises (proj-mgmt · Rocky8): Control, Monitoring stack, Replica DB
Cloud (AWS VPC): ALB, ASG (App), Bastion, Main DB
Connection (Tailscale L3): Bastion as subnet router, Direct on-prem↔VPC link with no public ports opened
Benefits: Private-network security, Use of on-prem resources, Unified observability across a single Tailnet

A Self-Healing Loop that automatically detects and recovers from failures:

This is the infrastructure track's key deliverable.

Before showing Track C's code structure, let me first explain DevSecOps.
DevSecOps combines DevOps with security. It is a methodology that embeds security into the entire lifecycle: planning, development, testing, deployment, operations, and monitoring.
Traditionally, teams moved fast through development and deployment, then crammed security checks into the final stage, which often delayed releases or letting security gaps slip through.
DevSecOps solves this with the core idea of "Shift-Left”. It pulls security earlier into development. In other words, it factors security in from the earliest planning and development stages, cutting cost and enabling fast, safe deployment.

True to our team name, Lock & Lock, we locked down security in 4 layers. Layer 1 is SAST, static code analysis; layer 2 is image vulnerability scanning; layer 3 is DAST, a dynamic check of the running app with ZAP; and layer 4 blocks real-time attacks at runtime via Nginx and Fail2ban.
Bandit is a static security testing (SAST) tool that analyzes Python source code without executing it. It finds security vulnerabilities and design flaws.
Trivy is a container scanning tool that finds known vulnerabilities in the OS packages and open-source libraries inside a Docker image.
OWASP ZAP (DAST) is a dynamic security testing (DAST) tool that runs simulated attacks against a live, running web application to find runtime vulnerabilities.
Explanation of layers 1, 2, and 3
Bandit (SAST): a static security testing (SAST) tool that analyzes Python source code without executing it, to find security vulnerabilities and design flaws.
Vulnerabilities Bandit detects are matched to standard CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) IDs in its report, making source-code-level defects easy to identify at a glance.
Trivy: a container scanning tool that finds known vulnerabilities in the OS packages and open-source libraries inside a Docker image.
Trivy links in real time to the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) data in NVD, the official vulnerability database maintained by the US government (NIST), to verify security flaws in the base image and build environment.
OWASP ZAP (DAST): a dynamic security testing (DAST) tool that runs simulated attacks against a live, running web application to find runtime vulnerabilities.
Because it scans against the 'OWASP Top 10’ (the most authoritative global standard for web application vulnerabilities), it's best suited for assessing risk in a real production environment.
1. SAST (Static Application Security Testing)
Meaning: a technique that finds security flaws by analyzing source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing the software (white-box testing). [1, 2]
Characteristics:
When tested: early in development (while coding or at build time)
Vulnerabilities found: code-level errors (SQL injection, hardcoded passwords, memory leaks, weak encryption, etc.)
Advantage: pinpoints the exact code line where the vulnerability occurs, enabling fast fixes.
2. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)
Meaning: a technique that injects input from the perspective of an outside attacker (black-box testing) while the software is running, to find abnormal behavior or vulnerabilities. [1, 2, 3]
Characteristics:
When tested: late in development (usually after deployment to a test or staging environment)
Vulnerabilities found: runtime environment issues (server misconfiguration, auth/authorization bypass, cookie and session vulnerabilities, etc.)
Advantage: uncovers potential attack paths that arise in a real production environment and structural vulnerabilities that only appear while running.
SAST (Static Application Security Testing): finds potential security vulnerabilities by analyzing the structure and patterns of source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing the application.
DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): detects runtime environment vulnerabilities by manipulating input and analyzing responses from the same perspective as an outside attacker while the application is running. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

We put the entire pipeline into this one slide. This shows the flow that automatically connects everything from the PR through security scanning, build/push, and to deployment.
CI/CD & DevSecOps Pipeline
When a developer pushes and the code lands in the GitHub repo, GitHub Actions runs code tests. Bandit inspects the source code for vulnerabilities and assigns each one a CWE ID.
Once the vulnerability check finishes, it builds the Docker image and runs Trivy to check for OS and package vulnerabilities inside the image.
After security verification completes, the image is pushed for the final time.
Deployment proceeds via a manual trigger button.
After deployment, OWASP ZAP launches attacks against the live URL.
After the attack run, it writes a security vulnerability report as a GitHub issue, reporting whatever vulnerabilities were found.
The team fixes the discovered vulnerabilities and does a final push.

The CI/CD code consists of the plan/deploy/destroy workflows, issue and PR templates, and deployment helper scripts. As shown at the bottom, this track acts as the hub connecting tracks. It consumes Track B's Docker images and Track A's Makefile targets.

Track D is the observability and auto-recovery stack. We built an observability stack of 11 containers (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and more), and implemented dual alerting via CloudWatch and Alertmanager, policy-based auto-recovery, and dynamic target discovery via Tailscale SD.

For monitoring, we separated Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Loki, the Recovery Controller, etc. into their own directories, and built a bootstrap script that queries AWS resources to configure everything automatically.
Prometheus & Grafana observability
Collects system metrics and custom metrics (failed login count, transfer request count, etc.) via Prometheus and visualizes them in real time on a Grafana dashboard.
Unified log collection via Loki & Promtail
Collects Nginx access/error logs, application logs, and system logs in real time and feeds them into the dashboard.
Self-healing Recovery Controller
Built a self-healing engine that, on alerts like BankAppDown, restarts containers and verifies health-check status via API, and immediately reports recovery success or failure over Telegram.
•  Unified log collection via Loki & Promtail: recovery logs and security event logs are collected by Promtail, stored in Loki, and queried in Grafana as an operational history
•  Pre-Verify based auto-recovery: checks status via health check before running recovery, and only restarts the remote container when there's an actual failure
•  Verify-based recovery outcome: re-checks the same endpoint after recovery to confirm the service is actually back to normal

Track E covers attack simulation and layered defense. We generated attack traffic with 3 Locust scenarios, defended in layers with Nginx rate limiting and Fail2ban, and responded automatically all the way from detection to alerting, blocking, and Telegram notification. We also documented our incident response procedure.
• Locust load & attack scenarios: Generates large-scale traffic requests with the load-testing tool (Locust) to validate the real-time blocking effectiveness of the Nginx and fail2ban defense mechanisms.
Locust load & attack scenarios: writes real attack scenarios (normal user traffic, brute-force login attempts, large-scale API flooding) to rigorously stress-test the system for security validation.
• Nginx rate limit: the Nginx web server watches per-client-IP request counts for each API and blocks immediately once a threshold is exceeded.
Nginx rate limit: when a sudden surge of API requests occurs, rate limiting kicks in, returning HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) and throttling requests to FastAPI.
• fail2ban automatic IP blocking: the host OS (fail2ban) uses regex to detect attacker IPs in Nginx's JSON logs, and automatically isolates them via firewall (iptables) rules once a threshold is exceeded
fail2ban automatic IP blocking: once failed login attempts exceed a threshold, it detects the pattern in the Nginx access log and automatically blocks that IP at the firewall in real time, sending a block notification.

The security code consists of attack scripts, policy documents, and validation scripts. Defense operates in two stages. The first stage is handled by Nginx: if requests spike within a short window, it throttles with a 429 response. Any IP that keeps hammering anyway gets isolated entirely at the second stage by Fail2ban via iptables. Fail2ban maintains three jails by attack type, each detecting and containing IPs for login brute-forcing, traffic flooding, and vulnerability scanning respectively.
① nginx-login : "If the same IP keeps failing logins (401), treat it as a brute-force attack and block it." A legitimate user might mistype a few times but succeeds soon after; a bot fails hundreds of times, revealing the pattern.
② nginx-rate-limit : "If an IP that Nginx rate limiting is already blocking with 429 keeps hammering, block the IP outright." This traps persistent IPs trying to punch through the first line of defense (Nginx 429).
③ nginx-scan : "Block IPs scanning paths that don't exist in our app, like WordPress or PHP admin pages." This stops automated scans attackers send looking for vulnerabilities before they ever reach the application.

This is the initial setup stage. Setup installs the tools and connects Tailscale, then checks if it acts as the gate. If there's a problem with credentials, Docker, or Tailscale, it blocks immediately before deployment to prevent incidents.

Full-service runs in three stages: Service builds the image and deploys infrastructure and app/DB. Then, on EC2 boot, the app starts itself and followed by the monitoring stack coming up, auto-configuring the entire environment.

Breaking down service: Builds the app & security Nginx images, pushes to Docker Hub, builds the bootstrap image, provisions infrastructure with Terraform, and deploys the DB with Ansible. The key part here is that the Tailscale IP gets auto-injected.

The app starts itself the moment EC2 boots, with no separate deploy command. user_data pulls the bootstrap image, extracts the app files, brings up Nginx, FastAPI, and the exporter, then sets up the 3 Fail2ban jails.

To sum up the results as metrics: ~60 Terraform resources auto-provisioned, 4-layer security lock across SAST/image/DAST/runtime, 6 layers passing E2E live verification GREEN, and 11 observability containers. We proved every scenario live from login-attack detection, blocking, and automatic container recovery.

We automated teardown. A single destroy command runs all 4 stages together: cleaning up monitoring AWS resources, removing the monitoring stack, cleaning up the Replica DB, and reclaiming the Terraform infrastructure.

In the end, a handful of Makefile-based commands covered the full operational cycle: building the container image, provisioning infrastructure, deploying the app, monitoring and recovery, and cleaning up resources.
This is the result of our team treating IaC-based operational automation as a core value.
The next topic is about our troubleshooting cases.

We organized the issues found and resolved across the whole project into 4 categories, totaling 6 issues: security detection, monitoring, infrastructure/deployment, and network. The shared lesson was that E2E live verification is what surfaced the gap between 'configured' and 'actually working.'

This is our first case. Failed logins were handled as 302 redirects, so no 401 ever appeared in the log and detection metrics sat at 0. We changed the response to 401 and unified/doubled the detection source on the Nginx 401 log, then confirmed with a live run from detection through the Fail2ban block.

After introducing the Nginx reverse proxy, Prometheus stopped properly collecting app status. We introduced a Blackbox Exporter-based health check to restructure detection around user-facing access rather than the app itself.

Docker Hub login conflicted with the host's global config, making builds and pushes unstable. We pinned DOCKER_CONFIG to a repo-isolated folder in the Makefile and dynamically parsed the login ID, achieving reproducible behavior on any machine.

Even after restarting the container, the service wasn't recovering. The initial logic only restarted the app and missed DB/network dependencies. We added Main/Replica DB connection checks and network verification to the recovery procedure and finished with a health-check step.

The login page rendered, but the processing never completed. The firewall/NAT environment was preventing the Tailscale tunnel between the app and Replica DB from initializing. We fixed it by pinging the app instance to register the connection with the firewall (hole punching) and establishing a direct P2P connection.

Right after we exposed the EC2 service, a flood of automated scans targeting WordPress/PHP web-shell vulnerabilities came in. We blocked it with an Nginx security policy that stops requests before they reach the application.
Case 6: Automated web-shell scanning right after going live on the internet
Right after exposing the EC2 service, a flood of automated scan requests targeting WordPress/PHP web-shell vulnerabilities came in.
We confirmed repeated access attempts against paths that don't exist.
We added an Nginx security policy that blocks PHP execution paths, blocks WordPress admin paths, and immediately returns 404 for unnecessary requests. This stopped them at the Nginx layer before they reached the application.
One-line summary for the talk
The moment we exposed EC2 to the internet, automated scan requests came in probing for WordPress web shells and admin pages. We responded by proactively blocking PHP/WordPress-related paths at Nginx so requests never reached the application.

In terms of real-world applicability, this can extend into fraud detection for finance/fintech, regulatory compliance via SAST/DAST, shorter incident MTTR through self-healing, and a hybrid operating model combining in-house resources with the cloud.

First, our team achieved the following on this project: security event detection, response, and self-recovery end to end, building a hybrid IaC infrastructure that uses Docker, and a 4-layer security lock (SAST, image, DAST, runtime). We ran the full login-attack path live from 401 detection through 429 blocking to Fail2ban.
There are four areas for future improvement: implementing DB security threat and failure recovery scenarios, completing Blue-Green zero-downtime deployment, achieving high availability through NAT Instance redundancy, and further strengthening security with L7/WAF blocking.

Finally, a few short reflections from the team. Something we all felt in common: security shouldn’t be an afterthought but a default we should design from the start.
Building security as a real, working system rather than just documentation helped us understand it as something that spans from blocking attacks to service stability and operational efficiency. This project broadened our view beyond infrastructure into security.
